zakarid-armenia.t: An Armenian principality under Georgian overlordship whose Zakarid princes reconquered Ani and sponsored an Armenian cultural revival around 1200.
zakarid-armenia.o: The brothers Zakare and Ivane, of an Armenian family that served the Georgian crown, became leading generals of Queen Tamar. After taking Ani in 1199 and other Seljuk-held lands, they were granted northern [[s:armenia|Armenia]] around 1201 as hereditary rulers under the [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]].
zakarid-armenia.r: Zakare held the title of commander-in-chief and Ivane of atabeg in the Georgian court. They ruled through Armenian nobles such as the Orbelians, Vachutians and Hasan-Jalalyans, and trade on routes through Ani and Dvin revived. A wave of building produced monasteries and churches at Harichavank, Haghartsin, Geghard and Ani. Ivane converted to Georgian Orthodoxy while Zakare stayed in the Armenian church.
zakarid-armenia.e: Khwarazmian and then Mongol invasions crushed this revival; by 1236 the Zakarids were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] and later the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]]. Their power shrank as the Mongol order collapsed, and by the 1360s [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] confederations had taken control of their lands.

zirid-emirate.t: The Sanhaja Berber dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya for the Fatimids, broke away, and was ruined by the Banu Hilal invasions.
zirid-emirate.o: When the Fatimid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Mu'izz moved to [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in 972, he left [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]] to Buluggin ibn Ziri, son of the Sanhaja [[e:berbers|Berber]] chief Ziri ibn Manad, who had served the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] loyally from his fortress at Ashir. The Zirids ruled from [[e:kairouan|Kairouan]] as hereditary governors of the [[s:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimid Caliphate]].
zirid-emirate.r: Under Zirid rule [[e:kairouan|Kairouan]] reached its height as a centre of trade, crafts and [[e:maliki-school|Maliki]] scholarship, and [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]] exported grain, [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]] and textiles. In 1015 the western lands broke away under the [[s:hammadid-emirate|Hammadid emirate]]. Around 1048 al-Mu'izz ibn Badis rejected Fatimid [[e:shiism|Shiism]] and recognised the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]], a move welcomed by the [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] majority.
zirid-emirate.e: In revenge the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] encouraged the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym Arab tribes to move west. They defeated the Zirids at Haydaran in 1052, and [[e:kairouan|Kairouan]] was abandoned in 1057. Confined to Mahdia and the coast, the dynasty ended in 1148 when the Normans of the [[s:kingdom-of-africa|Kingdom of Africa]] took Mahdia.

zoutpansberg-republic.t: A remote Boer republic in the far northern Transvaal built around the ivory-hunting town of Schoemansdal.
zoutpansberg-republic.o: Andries Hendrik Potgieter led his followers north from Ohrigstad in 1848 to the Soutpansberg mountains, where they founded the village later called Schoemansdal. After Potgieter's death in 1852 the community was led by his son Piet and then by Stephanus Schoeman, and it acted as a separate republic.
zoutpansberg-republic.r: Schoemansdal lived mainly from elephant hunting and the [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] trade with Delagoa Bay and Inhambane, using African hunters armed with guns. Its government was a small Volksraad and commandants. Relations with the neighbouring [[s:venda-kingdom|Venda Kingdom]] were tense, with raids, labour exactions and the capture of children for service.
zoutpansberg-republic.e: Zoutpansberg was merged into the [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]] in the early 1860s. As elephants were hunted out and Venda resistance grew, the [[e:boers|Boers]] abandoned and burned Schoemansdal in 1867.

zalmaqum.t: Zalmaqum, a league of small kingdoms around Harran in the Balikh valley, known from the Mari letters of the 18th century BCE.
zalmaqum.o: Zalmaqum was the name of a region of northern [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] around [[e:harran|Harran]] and the upper Balikh river. In the 18th century BCE its four kings acted together as a loose confederacy, alongside the Amorite tribal groups who moved seasonally through the steppe.
zalmaqum.r: The [[s:mari|Mari]] archives record that the kings of Zalmaqum and Yaminite tribal leaders swore an alliance in the temple of the moon god Sin at [[e:harran|Harran]], already an important sanctuary. They negotiated with [[e:mari|Mari]], [[s:yamhad|Yamhad]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia|Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia]], but no texts from the confederacy itself survive.
zalmaqum.e: The confederacy disappears from the record after the fall of [[s:mari|Mari]] c. 1760 BCE. [[e:harran|Harran]] remained a major city and centre of the moon cult into the Islamic period.

zande-kingdoms.t: A cluster of kingdoms ruled by the Avongara aristocracy across the Nile–Congo watershed, made famous by Evans-Pritchard's study of Zande witchcraft and oracles.
zande-kingdoms.o: From the 18th century the Ambomu people, led by the Avongara ruling clan, expanded east and south from the Mbomu river, conquering and assimilating many neighbouring peoples. As each Avongara ruler's sons founded their own domains, a patchwork of related but independent kingdoms emerged across the Uele and Mbomu basins.
zande-kingdoms.r: Each king ruled a central court and appointed sons and loyal commoners as provincial governors, keeping organised companies of young warriors. Zande society relied on farming and hunting and was noted for its use of poison oracles to settle disputes and identify witches. In the 19th century Zande kings fought Arab-Sudanese [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and slave traders and, later, the Mahdist state.
zande-kingdoms.e: The kingdoms were partitioned between the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]], French [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]] and [[s:anglo-egyptian-sudan|Anglo-Egyptian Sudan]]. Gbudwe, the most powerful king, was killed resisting British forces in 1905. E. E. Evans-Pritchard's 1937 study of the Azande became a classic of anthropology.

zeta-under-the-crnojevici.t: Last free Serbian Orthodox principality of the 15th-century Balkans, where Ivan Crnojević founded Cetinje and his son set up the first South Slav printing press.
zeta-under-the-crnojevici.o: After the decline of the Balšić lords and the [[s:serbian-despotate|Serbian Despotate]], the Crnojević family took the lead in the mountains of Zeta. Stefan Crnojević, ruling from around 1451, allied with [[e:venice|Venice]] and joined Skanderbeg's [[s:league-of-lezhe|League of Lezhë]], holding the territory around Lake Skadar and the highlands behind the Bay of [[s:commune-of-kotor|Kotor]].
zeta-under-the-crnojevici.r: The principality was a confederation of mountain clans led by a hereditary lord who balanced Venetian alliance against Ottoman pressure. Ivan Crnojević moved his seat from Žabljak to Cetinje in 1482 and founded a monastery there in 1484. His son Đurađ opened a [[e:printing-press|printing]] press that produced the Oktoih in 1494, among the first Cyrillic books printed.
zeta-under-the-crnojevici.e: Ottoman pressure forced Đurađ Crnojević to flee to [[e:venice|Venice]] in 1496, and Zeta was absorbed into the Ottoman sanjak of Scutari. Leadership of the highlands passed to the metropolitans of Cetinje, laying the ground for the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-montenegro|Prince-Bishopric of Montenegro]].

zululand-british-colony.t: The British colony created from the remnant of the Zulu kingdom in 1887, incorporated into Natal ten years later.
zululand-british-colony.o: After the Anglo-[[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]] War and the civil war that followed, [[e:boers|Boers]] had taken the western part of [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zululand]] as the [[s:nieuwe-republiek|Nieuwe Republiek]]. To prevent further losses, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] annexed the rest of Zululand in May 1887, ending the independence of the Zulu Kingdom.
zululand-british-colony.r: A resident commissioner, Sir Melmoth Osborn, governed from Eshowe through magistrates and appointed chiefs, and a hut tax was imposed. Dinuzulu, son of Cetshwayo, led resistance in 1888; he was tried for treason and exiled to St Helena. Many [[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]] men were drawn into migrant labour.
zululand-british-colony.e: [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zululand]] was annexed to the [[s:natal-colony|Natal Colony]] in December 1897. A land commission then opened much of it to white settlement, while the remaining reserves later formed the core of the KwaZulu homeland.

zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen.t: The Abdalwadid kingdom of Tlemcen, a Zenata Berber state that held the central Maghreb and a key terminus of the Saharan gold trade for three centuries.
zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen.o: The Banu Abd al-Wad, a Zenata [[e:berbers|Berber]] tribe, served the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] in the region of [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]]. As [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] power faded, their chief Yaghmurasan ibn Zayyan took control of the city in 1235 and soon ruled independently, fending off both the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsid Sultanate]] to the east and the rising [[s:marinid-sultanate|Marinids]] to the west.
zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen.r: [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]] sat where [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] from [[e:sijilmasa|Sijilmasa]] and the [[e:sahara|Sahara]] reached the ports of Oran and Honaine, trading gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and slaves for European cloth. The court patronised scholars, built mosques and [[e:madrasa|madrasas]], and hosted a large Jewish community. Abu Hammu Musa II was himself a poet and author of a manual on kingship.
zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen.e: The kingdom endured repeated Marinid sieges and occupations, including 1337 to 1348 and 1352 to 1359. [[s:spanish-oran|Spanish Oran]] from 1509 and the corsairs of the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]] then reduced it to a contested [[e:vassal|vassal]], and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] annexed [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]] definitively in the 1550s.

zaghawa-sultanates.t: A cluster of small Zaghawa sultanates on the Darfur-Chad frontier, including Kobe, Dar Tuar and Dar Gala, caught between Darfur and Wadai.
zaghawa-sultanates.o: The [[e:zaghawa|Zaghawa]] are a Saharan people of the borderlands between [[e:chad|Chad]] and [[e:sudan|Sudan]], mentioned by Arabic writers from the 9th century. By the 17th century several Zaghawa chieftaincies had formed sultanates, among them Kobe, Dar Tuar and Dar Gala, in the semi-desert north of [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] and [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]].
zaghawa-sultanates.r: The sultanates were small, with rulers drawn from leading lineages governing [[e:camel|camel]]-herding clans and some farming communities. They paid tribute to the [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]] or the [[s:wadai-empire|Wadai Empire]] and supplied them with soldiers. [[e:islam|Islam]] spread among them, mixed with older practices, and they controlled routes toward [[e:libya|Libya]].
zaghawa-sultanates.e: French troops occupied [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]] from 1909, and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] annexed [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] in 1916. The Anglo-French border settlement split the [[e:zaghawa|Zaghawa]] between [[e:chad|Chad]] and [[e:sudan|Sudan]], and their sultans became traditional chiefs under colonial rule.

zhai-wei.t: A short-lived Dingling state on the Yellow River in Henan, founded by Zhai Liao amid the wreck of Former Qin and crushed by Later Yan in 392.
zhai-wei.o: The Zhai clan led Dingling tribesmen, a Turkic-speaking people related to the later [[s:gaoche|Gaoche]], who had been settled in northern [[e:china|China]]. After the collapse of [[s:former-qin|Former Qin]], Zhai [[e:liao-dynasty|Liao]] switched allegiance several times before taking Huatai (modern Hua County, Henan) in 388 and proclaiming himself Heavenly King of Wei.
zhai-wei.r: Zhai Wei was a small military state holding a stretch of the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]] valley between [[s:later-yan|Later Yan]] and the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]]. Little is known of its administration. Zhai [[e:liao-dynasty|Liao]] died in 391 and was succeeded by his son Zhai Zhao.
zhai-wei.e: In 392 Murong Chui of [[s:later-yan|Later Yan]] forced a crossing of the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]], defeated Zhai Zhao and took Huatai. Zhai Zhao fled to [[s:western-yan|Western Yan]] and was later killed, and the Dingling of the region were absorbed into Later Yan.

zenu.t: Chiefdoms of Colombia's Caribbean lowlands that built a vast network of drained fields and canals and produced some of the finest goldwork of pre-Columbian America.
zenu.o: The Zenú, or Sinú, lived in the floodplains of the Sinú and San Jorge rivers and the Mojana depression in northern [[s:republic-of-colombia|Colombia]]. From around 200 BCE they began building an extensive system of parallel canals and raised ridges to control seasonal flooding, eventually covering hundreds of thousands of hectares.
zenu.r: Spanish accounts describe three linked provinces, Finzenú, Panzenú and Zenufana, each ruled by a chief. The hydraulic works supported dense farming of [[e:maize|maize]] and [[e:cassava|cassava]], as well as fishing. The Zenú were skilled goldsmiths, casting filigree earrings and figurines, and their burial mounds held rich gold offerings. They also wove fibre from cane flecha, a skill that survives in the modern sombrero vueltiao.
zenu.e: The canal system had largely gone out of use by about 1000 CE, but Zenú society persisted. Spaniards from Cartagena looted their tombs from 1534, and colonial rule, disease and forced labour broke up the chiefdoms. Zenú descendants live today in the reserve of San Andrés de Sotavento.

zamua.t: The Assyrian name for the hill lands around the Shahrizor plain, whose chiefs resisted Ashurnasirpal II before becoming an Assyrian province.
zamua.o: Zamua, or Mazamua, covered the plain of Shahrizor and the valleys around modern Sulaymaniyah, the old homeland of the [[s:lullubi|Lullubi]]. In the 9th century BCE it was divided among local rulers who controlled the passes between the [[e:tigris|Tigris]] lowlands and the [[e:iranian-plateau|Iranian plateau]].
zamua.r: Zamua is known almost entirely from Assyrian royal annals. Ashurnasirpal II campaigned there in the 880s BCE against a coalition led by Nur-Adad, a chief of Dagara, and later against Ameka and Arashtua, destroying fortified towns and imposing tribute of horses, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and wine. Its lands were valued for livestock and as a route east.
zamua.e: By the late 9th century [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] had turned Mazamua into a province, governed from Assyrian forts. It remained part of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] until the empire collapsed in 612 to 609 BCE.

zasagt-khanate.t: The western of the three Khalkha khanates of Outer Mongolia, whose feud with the Tüsheet Khan triggered the Dzungar invasion and Khalkha submission to the Qing.
zasagt-khanate.o: Dayan Khan of the [[s:northern-yuan|Northern Yuan]] gave the Khalkha [[e:mongols|Mongols]] of northern [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]] to his youngest son Geresenje, whose sons divided them into [[e:appanage|appanages]]. In the late 16th century the western Khalkha under one branch of his descendants took the title Zasagt Khan, ruling the lands towards the Khangai and [[e:altai-mountains|Altai]] mountains.
zasagt-khanate.r: The khanate was a federation of noble-led nomad groups under a Chinggisid khan, with no fixed capital. It bordered the [[e:oirats|Oirats]] and later the [[s:dzungar-khanate|Dzungar Khanate]], and its khans also had influence on the Khotogoid and other western groups. Like the rest of Khalkha it adopted Gelug [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] in this period.
zasagt-khanate.e: Disputes over subjects between the Zasagt and Tüsheet khans led to war in 1687, in which the Zasagt Khan was killed. The [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] ruler Galdan used this as a pretext to invade Khalkha in 1688, and at Dolon Nor in 1691 the Khalkha nobles submitted to the [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]], which reorganised them as banners.

zurayid-dynasty.t: An Isma'ili dynasty that ruled the port of Aden and grew rich on Indian Ocean trade between the Sulayhid and Ayyubid eras.
zurayid-dynasty.o: The Banu Zuray, a branch of the Yam tribe of Hamdan, were appointed governors of Aden by the [[s:sulayhid-dynasty|Sulayhid dynasty]] around 1083, when the brothers al-Abbas and al-Mas'ud ibn Karam shared the city. As Sulayhid power faded under Queen Arwa they became independent rulers.
zurayid-dynasty.r: The Zurayids profited from Aden's role as the main port between [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and [[e:india|India]]; the documents of the [[e:cairo|Cairo]] Geniza describe Jewish and Muslim merchants trading [[e:pepper|pepper]], textiles and metals through the harbour. They followed the Hafizi branch of [[e:ismailism|Isma'ilism]], recognised by the Fatimid court in Cairo. Saba ibn Abi al-Su'ud consolidated their rule in the 1130s and they extended inland to Ta'izz and Dhu Jibla.
zurayid-dynasty.e: In 1174 the Ayyubid prince Turan-Shah invaded [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] and took Aden, ending the dynasty. Aden remained [[e:yemen|Yemen's]] chief port under [[s:ayyubid-yemen|Ayyubid Yemen]] and the [[s:rasulid-dynasty|Rasulid dynasty]].

zubayrs-bahr-al-ghazal.t: The private trading and slaving empire of the merchant Zubayr Rahma Mansur in south-western Sudan, which grew strong enough to conquer Darfur.
zubayrs-bahr-al-ghazal.o: Zubayr Rahma Mansur, a Ja'ali merchant from the [[e:nile|Nile]], entered the Bahr al-Ghazal region around 1856 to trade in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] under the [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]]. He built a chain of fortified stations, called zaribas, and made Dem Zubayr his headquarters, forming alliances with local [[s:zande-kingdoms|Azande]] and other chiefs.
zubayrs-bahr-al-ghazal.r: Zubayr's power rested on a private army of enslaved soldiers armed with firearms, known as bazingers. His network traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and enslaved people north to [[e:kordofan|Kordofan]] and [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. He defeated an Egyptian force sent against him, and in 1873 the [[s:khedivate-of-egypt|Khedivate of Egypt]] recognised him as governor of the Bahr al-Ghazal.
zubayrs-bahr-al-ghazal.e: In 1874 Zubayr invaded the [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]], killing [[e:ibrahim-of-darfur|Sultan Ibrahim]] and handing the country to [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. Detained in [[e:cairo|Cairo]] from 1875, he lost control of his domain; his son Sulayman rebelled and was killed in 1879.

zacazgo-of-hunza.t: The northern Muisca realm of the zaque, ruled from Hunza, the site of modern Tunja, and long the rival of the zipa of Bacatá.
zacazgo-of-hunza.o: [[s:hunza-state|Hunza]], now Tunja in Boyacá, became the seat of the zaque, ruler of the northern [[s:muisca-confederation|Muisca]] territories, in the centuries before the Spanish conquest. Muisca tradition named Hunzahúa as its first ruler and claimed the zaques descended from him.
zacazgo-of-hunza.r: The zaque ruled through lesser chiefs and received tribute in gold, cloth and goods. Succession passed from a ruler to his sister's son. [[s:hunza-state|Hunza]] was a centre of trade in salt, emeralds, [[e:cotton|cotton]] and gold. The zaques fought repeated wars with the zipas of the [[s:zipazgo-of-bacata|Zipazgo of Bacatá]], including a battle in which the zipa Saguamanchica and the zaque Michuá were both killed around 1490.
zacazgo-of-hunza.e: In 1537 Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada seized [[s:hunza-state|Hunza]] and captured the aged zaque Quemuenchatocha. His successor Aquiminzaque was executed in 1540. The Spanish founded Tunja on the site in 1539, and it became a major town of the [[s:new-kingdom-of-granada|New Kingdom of Granada]].

zapotec-kingdom-of-tehuantepec.t: The last independent Zapotec kingdom, on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, which withstood an Aztec siege at the fortress of Guiengola.
zapotec-kingdom-of-tehuantepec.o: In the late 15th century the Zapotec king Cocijoeza of [[s:zaachila|Zaachila]] conquered the Isthmus of Tehuantepec from Mixe, Zoque and Huave peoples and moved his royal seat there, around 1490, gaining control of the trade route between central [[s:mexico|Mexico]] and Soconusco.
zapotec-kingdom-of-tehuantepec.r: The [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] under [[e:ahuitzotl|Ahuitzotl]] sought to seize the isthmus, but Cocijoeza held out at the mountain fortress of Guiengola in a long siege in the late 1490s. Peace was sealed by his marriage to an Aztec princess, and their son Cocijopii succeeded him. The kingdom ruled a mixed population of Zapotecs and other peoples in a rich lowland.
zapotec-kingdom-of-tehuantepec.e: Cocijopii submitted to the Spanish around 1521 and was baptised Juan [[e:hernan-cortes|Cortés]] Cocijopii, keeping noble rank. Tehuantepec became a colonial town within [[s:new-spain|New Spain]], and the isthmus remains a stronghold of Zapotec culture.

zheng-wang-shichong.t: The regime of the Sui general Wang Shichong at Luoyang, whose defeat by Li Shimin in 621 decided the struggle for the Sui succession in favour of the Tang.
zheng-wang-shichong.o: Wang Shichong, a general of Central Asian descent, defended [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] for [[e:emperor-yang-of-sui|Emperor Yang]] against the rebel Li Mi. After the emperor's murder in 618 he and other officials enthroned the young Yang Tong as [[e:sui-dynasty|Sui]] emperor; Wang crushed Li Mi's Wagang army and in 619 forced Yang Tong to abdicate, proclaiming the state of [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]].
zheng-wang-shichong.r: [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]] held [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] and much of Henan, but Wang governed through suspicion and harsh punishments, and the deposed Yang Tong was soon killed. Long sieges brought famine to Luoyang, and many officers defected to the [[s:later-tang|Tang]]. The regime had little time to build institutions of its own.
zheng-wang-shichong.e: From 620 [[e:emperor-taizong-of-tang|Li Shimin]] besieged [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]]. After he defeated and captured the relieving army of Dou Jiande at Hulao in 621, Wang Shichong surrendered. He was spared and sent into exile but murdered on the way by Dugu Xiude, whose father Wang had executed. His fall gave the [[s:tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] the eastern heartland.

ziyarid-dynasty.t: A Gilite dynasty of the Caspian lands whose founder dreamed of restoring the Persian empire and whose prince Qabus built the soaring tower of Gonbad-e Qabus.
ziyarid-dynasty.o: Mardavij ibn Ziyar, a Gilite commander who had served Daylamite warlords, seized Tabaristan and Gorgan and then the Jibal around 931. He ruled from [[e:isfahan|Isfahan]], celebrated old Iranian festivals such as Sadeh and was said to plan the conquest of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] and a revived Sasanian monarchy. His Turkish slave guards murdered him in 935.
ziyarid-dynasty.r: His brother Vushmgir kept Gorgan and Tabaristan, while the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyid dynasty]], once Mardavij's officers, took the Jibal. Qabus ibn Vushmgir, ruler in 977 to 981 and 997 to 1012, was a learned prince and stylist in Arabic, patron of al-Biruni, and built the brick tomb tower Gonbad-e Qabus in 1006 to 1007. His grandson Keikavus wrote the Qabus-nama, a classic Persian book of advice for princes.
ziyarid-dynasty.e: The Ziyarids became [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]] and then the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]]. The dynasty faded around 1090, when its last prince, Gilanshah, lost his lands, reportedly to the [[e:nizari-ismaili-state|Nizari Ismailis]].

zalpa.t: Zalpa, a city-state on the Black Sea coast that rivalled Nesa and figures in the oldest Hittite legend, the tale of the queen of Kanesh's thirty sons.
zalpa.o: Zalpuwa lay on the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] near the mouth of the Kızılırmak river. In the early 2nd millennium BCE it was one of the native Anatolian kingdoms competing for power with [[s:kanesh|Kanesh]], and the [[e:hittite-empire|Hittites]] remembered it in a legend of thirty sons of the queen of [[e:kanesh|Kanesh]] who drifted there in baskets.
zalpa.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. The Anitta text records that Uhna, king of Zalpuwa, carried off the statue of the god of Nesa, and that Anitta later captured Huzziya of Zalpuwa and brought the statue home.
zalpa.e: Zalpa resisted the early Hittite kings for years. According to the Hittite Zalpa text, it was besieged and finally destroyed in the time of [[e:hattusili-i|Hattusili I]], c. 1650 BCE, and its land became part of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]].

zunbils.t: Rulers of Zabulistan in southern Afghanistan who resisted Arab conquest for two centuries, defeating several caliphal armies.
zunbils.o: The Zunbil dynasty emerged in the late 7th century in the region of Zabul, between Ghazni and [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]], possibly as a branch of the [[s:turk-shahis|Turk Shahis]] or of Hephthalite origin. The title Zunbil is often linked to the sun god Zun, whose shrine at Zamindawar was a famous pilgrimage site.
zunbils.r: The Zunbils ruled a mountainous territory with a mixed [[e:hinduism|Hindu]], Buddhist and Zun-worshipping population. They fought the Umayyad governors of Sistan for decades and in 698 destroyed the so-called 'Army of Destruction' sent by al-Hajjaj, an event that helped trigger the revolt of Ibn al-Ash'ath. Paying intermittent tribute, they kept effective independence.
zunbils.e: In 865 Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, founder of the [[s:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarid dynasty]], killed the reigning Zunbil, and by about 870 he had conquered Zabulistan. The region was Islamised under the [[e:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarids]] and later became the heartland of the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]].

zulu-kingdom.t: The kingdom Shaka built from a small chiefdom, whose regimental army dominated southeastern Africa and defeated Britain at Isandlwana.
zulu-kingdom.o: In 1816 Shaka seized the leadership of the small Zulu chiefdom with the backing of Dingiswayo of the [[s:mthethwa-paramountcy|Mthethwa Paramountcy]]. After Dingiswayo was killed by Zwide of the [[s:ndwandwe-kingdom|Ndwandwe Kingdom]], Shaka defeated the Ndwandwe around 1819 and absorbed the Mthethwa and many neighbouring chiefdoms into a single kingdom between the Phongolo and Thukela rivers.
zulu-kingdom.r: The king commanded age-based regiments, amabutho, quartered in royal homesteads and armed with the short stabbing spear and large shield. [[e:cattle|Cattle]] raided or received as tribute underpinned royal power, and regiments could marry only with royal permission. Shaka was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brother Dingane, who fought the Voortrekkers at Blood River in 1838; Mpande and then Cetshwayo, who built his capital at Ulundi, ruled after him.
zulu-kingdom.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] invaded in 1879, and after the Zulu victory at Isandlwana the army was broken at Ulundi. Zululand was split into thirteen chiefdoms, civil war followed, and in 1887 [[e:britain|Britain]] annexed it as [[s:zululand-british-colony|Zululand (British colony)]]. The Zulu monarchy survives as a traditional institution.

zanj-state.t: The rebel state of enslaved East Africans in the marshes near Basra, which defied the Abbasid Caliphate for fourteen years and sacked Basra.
zanj-state.o: Thousands of enslaved East Africans, called Zanj, were forced to clear the salt-encrusted soil of the marshes around [[e:basra|Basra]] for farming. In 869 Ali ibn Muhammad, a man of disputed background who claimed descent from Ali, raised them in revolt, promising freedom and wealth. The rebels built a fortified capital, al-Mukhtara, among the canals of the Shatt al-Arab region.
zanj-state.r: The rebellion became a state with its own leader, coinage and administration, exploiting the marshes to evade Abbasid armies. It drew on Kharijite slogans about equality, though former slaves acquired slaves of their own. The Zanj sacked [[e:basra|Basra]] in 871 with great slaughter and took Wasit and Ahvaz, cutting [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] off from the Gulf and its revenues.
zanj-state.e: The Abbasid regent al-Muwaffaq and his son, the future [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Mu'tadid, built a fleet and siege city opposite al-Mukhtara and stormed it in 883; Ali ibn Muhammad was killed. The revolt deeply weakened the [[e:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate's]] finances.

zhangzhung.t: The ancient kingdom of western Tibet around Mount Kailash, remembered as the homeland of the Bon religion, conquered by the Tibetan Empire in the 7th century.
zhangzhung.o: Zhangzhung was a kingdom of the high plateau of western [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] and [[s:kingdom-of-ladakh|Ladakh]], centred on the valley of Khyunglung near Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar. Archaeology shows fortified settlements and elite burials there from the 1st millennium BCE, but the kingdom's early history is known mainly from much later Tibetan, especially Bon, tradition.
zhangzhung.r: Bon texts present Zhangzhung as the land where the teacher Tonpa Shenrab's religion first flourished, and they preserve words of its Tibeto-Burman language. Its economy rested on herding, barley farming in sheltered valleys and trade routes linking [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]], [[e:india|India]] and [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]]. Old Tibetan annals treat it as a major rival of the Yarlung kings.
zhangzhung.e: Songtsen Gampo allied with Zhangzhung by marrying his sister to its king, Lig Myirhya, then conquered it around 644, making it a province of the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]]. Its language died out, but its memory remained central to Bon identity.

zipazgo-of-bacata.t: The southern Muisca realm of the zipa, centred on the savanna of Bogotá, the most powerful native state in Colombia when the Spanish arrived.
zipazgo-of-bacata.o: Bacatá, on the high savanna where Bogotá now stands, became the seat of the zipa, ruler of the southern [[s:muisca-confederation|Muisca]], in the 15th century. Muisca tradition names Meicuchuca as an early zipa, and Saguamanchica expanded the realm by conquering neighbouring chiefdoms such as Fusagasugá.
zipazgo-of-bacata.r: The zipa ruled through subordinate chiefs who paid tribute and supplied warriors. Succession went from uncle to nephew, and heirs were trained in seclusion. Nemequene, who reigned in the early 16th century, is credited with a code of laws. The realm controlled the salt mines of Zipaquirá and Nemocón, whose salt was traded widely. Lake Guatavita, a sacred lake, lay within its territory. Wars with the zaque of the [[s:zacazgo-of-hunza|Zacazgo of Hunza]] were frequent.
zipazgo-of-bacata.e: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada entered the savanna in 1537. The zipa Tisquesusa died fighting that year, and his successor Sagipa died in Spanish captivity in 1539 after being tortured for gold. Santa Fe de Bogotá was founded in 1538 as capital of the [[s:new-kingdom-of-granada|New Kingdom of Granada]].

zimbabwe-rhodesia.t: The short-lived state of 1979 created by the Internal Settlement, with a black prime minister but whites still holding key powers.
zimbabwe-rhodesia.o: Under the Internal Settlement of 1978 between Ian Smith and moderate African leaders, elections with universal suffrage were held in April 1979. [[s:rhodesia|Rhodesia]] was renamed [[e:zimbabwe|Zimbabwe]] Rhodesia on 1 June 1979, with [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Abel Muzorewa as prime minister and Josiah Zion Gumede as president.
zimbabwe-rhodesia.r: The constitution reserved 28 of 100 parliamentary seats for whites and left the army, police, judiciary and civil service in white hands. The Patriotic Front of Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo, excluded from the elections, kept fighting, and no country recognised the new state.
zimbabwe-rhodesia.e: Talks at Lancaster House in [[e:london|London]] produced an agreement in December 1979. The state returned to British rule under Lord Soames, and after elections won by Mugabe's ZANU-PF the country became independent as [[e:zimbabwe|Zimbabwe]] on 18 April 1980.

zaachila.t: The leading Zapotec kingdom of the Valley of Oaxaca after Monte Albán, whose kings later carried Zapotec power to Tehuantepec.
zaachila.o: Zaachila, called Teozapotlan by the Nahuas, emerged as the main Zapotec royal seat in the Valley of Oaxaca in the Postclassic period, from around 1100, filling the gap left by the decline of [[s:monte-alban|Monte Albán]].
zaachila.r: Its rulers held the highest prestige among Zapotec lords, and [[s:mitla|Mitla]] served as its religious centre. Zaachila was linked by marriage and rivalry to Mixtec lords, who settled in parts of the valley. Two decorated tombs excavated in 1962 contained Mixtec-style gold, turquoise and polychrome pottery. In the late 15th century King Cocijoeza resisted the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] and allied with it through marriage.
zaachila.e: Cocijoeza moved the royal seat to [[s:zapotec-kingdom-of-tehuantepec|Tehuantepec]], and Zaachila lost importance. The Spanish took control of the valley around 1521, and Zaachila became a colonial town.

zaria-emirate.t: The Fulani emirate that replaced the Hausa kingdom of Zazzau, a southern frontier of the Sokoto Caliphate and a major source of slaves.
zaria-emirate.o: In 1808 [[e:fula|Fulani]] forces led by Mallam Musa, a follower of [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio]], took [[e:zaria|Zaria]], capital of the [[s:kingdom-of-zazzau|Kingdom of Zazzau]]. The [[e:hausa|Hausa]] ruler fled south and founded the [[s:abuja-emirate|Abuja Emirate]]. Musa became the first Fulani emir of Zaria, ruling until 1821.
zaria-emirate.r: The emirship rotated among several [[e:fula|Fulani]] dynasties, the Mallawa, Bornawa, Katsinawa and later Sullubawa, with [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]] confirming each choice, a system that caused frequent rivalry. [[e:zaria|Zaria]] was one of the largest [[e:emirate|emirates]] in area, and its southern frontier with the peoples of the Nigerian Middle Belt was a zone of [[e:slave-raiding|slave raiding]] that supplied labour and tribute for Sokoto.
zaria-emirate.e: British forces took [[e:zaria|Zaria]] in 1902, and [[e:emir|Emir]] Kwassau was deposed in 1903 for resisting British authority. The [[e:emirate|emirate]] became part of the [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]], and the Emir of [[s:kingdom-of-zazzau|Zazzau]] still reigns in Kaduna State.

zhongjia.t: The short-lived empire of the warlord Yuan Shu, who proclaimed himself emperor in 197 and so became the most despised of the Han warlords.
zhongjia.o: Yuan Shu, of the powerful Yuan family, controlled the Huai River region in the chaos after the fall of Dong Zhuo. Possessing the imperial seal, taken from Sun Jian's family, and citing prophecies, he proclaimed himself emperor of Zhongjia at Shouchun in 197, while the Han emperor still lived.
zhongjia.r: The regime was notorious for extravagance: Yuan Shu's palace was said to keep hundreds of concubines in [[e:silk|silk]] while famine reduced his soldiers to eating shellfish. His usurpation lost him allies such as Sun Ce, and [[e:cao-cao|Cao Cao]], Lü Bu and others turned against him.
zhongjia.e: Defeated by Lü Bu and [[e:cao-cao|Cao Cao]], his territory collapsing, Yuan Shu set out in 199 to join his cousin Yuan Shao in the north, was blocked and died, reportedly asking in vain for honey water. His claim illustrated how far Han authority had decayed.

zhangchu.t: The short-lived regime of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, leaders of the first great peasant rising in Chinese history, which set the Qin empire ablaze.
zhangchu.o: In 209 BCE a party of [[e:conscription|conscripts]] led by Chen Sheng and Wu Guang was held up by rain at Dazexiang in Anhui. Facing execution for lateness under [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] law, they rebelled, asking whether kings and nobles were born to their station. Chen Sheng took the city of Chen and proclaimed himself king of Zhangchu, 'Expanding Chu', reviving the name of the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]].
zhangchu.r: Zhangchu was more a rebel movement than a state. Chen Sheng sent generals in all directions, and in the turmoil the kingdoms of Zhao, Wei, Qi and Yan were revived under their own kings. His general Zhou Wen came within reach of the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] capital before being driven back by the Qin commander Zhang Han.
zhangchu.e: Wu Guang was murdered by his own officers at Xingyang, and late in 209 or early in 208 BCE Chen Sheng was killed by his charioteer, Zhuang Jia, as Zhang Han's armies advanced. The rising had shown the [[s:qin-dynasty|Qin dynasty]] could be defeated, and other rebels, including [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] and [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]], carried it on.

zachlumia.t: Medieval principality of Hum in Herzegovina and southern Dalmatia, home of the Miroslav Gospel and contested by Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia.
zachlumia.o: Hum emerged among [[e:slavs|Slavs]] settled between the Neretva and Dubrovnik in the 7th to 9th centuries. Its best-known early ruler, Mihajlo Višević, governed in the early 10th century, allied with Simeon I of the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]] and attending church councils at Split.
zachlumia.r: Princes ruled from Ston and Bona near Blagaj, over a population divided between Catholic and [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] churches. Hum often fell under neighbours: [[s:duklja|Duklja]], the [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102|Kingdom of Croatia]] and later the [[s:grand-principality-of-serbia|Grand Principality of Serbia]]. Prince Miroslav, brother of Stefan Nemanja, ruled it in the late 12th century and commissioned the Miroslav Gospel, a masterpiece of Cyrillic illumination.
zachlumia.e: In 1326 Stephen II Kotromanić of the [[s:banate-of-bosnia|Banate of Bosnia]] took most of Hum, and in 1333 Ston and Pelješac were sold to the [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Republic of Ragusa]]. The region later became the core of Herzegovina.

zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.t: The Zaydi Shi'a imamate founded at Sa'dah in 897, a religious state in the northern Yemeni highlands that lasted, in various forms, until 1962.
zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.o: In 897 Yahya ibn al-Husayn, a descendant of al-Hasan from the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Hejaz]], came to Sa'dah at the invitation of feuding tribes. As [[e:imam|Imam]] al-Hadi ila al-Haqq he settled their disputes and founded a Zaydi state, establishing the doctrine that any learned descendant of Ali and [[e:fatima|Fatima]] who claimed the [[e:imamate|imamate]] by rising against injustice could be imam.
zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.r: The [[e:imamate|imamate]] had no hereditary succession; rival claimants often contested it, and its reach rarely extended far beyond the northern highlands and Sa'dah. [[e:imam|Imams]] depended on the support of tribes such as Hashid and Bakil. al-Mansur Abd Allah ibn Hamza in the 13th century revived its strength against the [[e:ayyubid-empire|Ayyubids]], and it competed with the [[s:sulayhid-dynasty|Sulayhids]], [[s:rasulid-dynasty|Rasulids]] and [[s:tahirid-dynasty|Tahirids]].
zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.e: [[e:imam|Imam]] Sharaf al-Din Yahya expanded the state in the early 16th century, but the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] conquered most of [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] after 1538. In 1597 al-Qasim ibn Muhammad proclaimed himself imam and began the revolt that created the [[s:qasimid-state|Qasimid State]].

zagwe-dynasty.t: The Agaw kings of Lasta who ruled Christian Ethiopia between Aksum and the Solomonic dynasty and carved the rock churches of Lalibela.
zagwe-dynasty.o: After the decline of the [[e:aksumite-empire|Kingdom of Aksum]], power shifted south to the Agaw people of Lasta. Around 1137, by the date usually given, an Agaw lord traditionally named [[e:mara-takla-haymanot|Mara Takla Haymanot]] took the throne, founding the Zagwe line. Later Solomonic writers treated the dynasty as usurpers, so its beginnings are poorly recorded and other chronologies place it earlier.
zagwe-dynasty.r: The Zagwe kings were devout Christians who kept close ties with the Coptic Church of [[e:alexandria|Alexandria]], which sent the head of the Ethiopian church. Their capital at Roha, later renamed [[e:lalibela|Lalibela]], became a pilgrimage centre. King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela, c. 1181 to 1221, is credited with its eleven monolithic churches cut from the rock, conceived as a new [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]]. Trade with the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] continued through Muslim intermediaries.
zagwe-dynasty.e: In 1270 [[e:yekuno-amlak|Yekuno Amlak]], a noble from [[e:amhara|Amhara]] claiming descent from [[e:solomon|Solomon]] and the Aksumite kings, overthrew the last Zagwe king, founding the Solomonic line of the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]]. Rulers of Wag, with the title wagshum, later claimed Zagwe descent, and the churches of [[e:lalibela|Lalibela]] remain in use as a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

zancle.t: Greek city on the Strait of Messina, named after its sickle-shaped harbour and renamed Messana in the 5th century BCE, which controlled the passage between Sicily and Italy.
zancle.o: Settlers from [[s:cumae|Cumae]] and [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]] founded Zancle in the second half of the 8th century BCE, at first as a base of '[[e:piracy|pirates]]', on the sickle-shaped peninsula that gave the city its name (zanklon, sickle). Facing [[s:rhegion|Rhegion]] across the Strait, it commanded one of the most important sea passages of the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
zancle.r: Zancle founded Mylae and [[s:himera|Himera]] and grew rich on traffic through the Strait. Around 490 BCE refugees from [[s:samos|Samos]] seized it, and soon afterwards Anaxilas, tyrant of [[s:rhegion|Rhegion]], took it, settled Messenians from the Peloponnese and renamed it [[s:mamertine-messana|Messana]]. It was later a democracy, sided at times with [[s:athens|Athens]], and was destroyed by the Carthaginian general [[e:himilco|Himilco]] in 396 BCE before Dionysius I refounded it.
zancle.e: In 288 BCE Campanian [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]], the [[s:mamertine-messana|Mamertines]], seized Messana and killed or expelled many citizens. Their appeal to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 264 BCE triggered the [[e:first-punic-war|First Punic War]]. The city became Roman Messana and is today Messina.

zeta-under-the-balsici.t: Principality of the Balšić family on the shores of Lake Skadar and the Adriatic, a successor of the Serbian Empire contested with Venice and the Ottomans.
zeta-under-the-balsici.o: Around 1356, after Stefan Dušan's death, Balša I and his sons Stracimir, Đurađ I and Balša II took control of Zeta, the land around Lake Skadar and the Gulf of [[s:commune-of-kotor|Kotor]], ruling from Skadar (Shkodër).
zeta-under-the-balsici.r: The Balšići ruled as lords of Zeta with nobles and coastal towns, fighting [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]], Bosnia and Albanian lords. Balša II took Valona and Durrës, but died fighting the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] at Savra in 1385. His successor Đurađ II Stracimirović gave Skadar to [[e:venice|Venice]] in 1396 to escape Ottoman pressure. Balša III fought long wars with Venice over Skadar and the coast.
zeta-under-the-balsici.e: Balša III died in 1421, leaving Zeta to his uncle, Despot Stefan Lazarević of [[s:serbia|Serbia]]. [[e:venice|Venice]] kept the coastal towns, and the inland region later became the Principality of Zeta under the Crnojević family.

zengid-dynasty-of-mosul.t: The senior line of the Zengids, who ruled Mosul after Zengi's capture of Edessa and left the city its great Nuri mosque.
zengid-dynasty-of-mosul.o: In 1127 the Seljuk sultan appointed Imad al-Din Zengi atabeg of [[e:mosul|Mosul]]. Zengi added [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] in 1128 and captured [[s:county-of-edessa|Edessa]] in 1144, destroying the County of Edessa and provoking the Second [[e:crusade|Crusade]]. After his murder in 1146 his lands were divided: [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] took Aleppo and [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], forming the [[s:zengid-dynasty|Zengid dynasty]], while Mosul passed to his son Sayf al-Din [[e:ghazi|Ghazi]] I.
zengid-dynasty-of-mosul.r: The [[e:mosul|Mosul]] [[s:zengid-dynasty|Zengids]] were Turkish rulers of an Arab, Kurdish and Christian population, governing through atabeg households and patronising [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] learning, architecture and metalwork, for which Mosul was famed. Qutb al-Din Mawdud ruled from 1149 to 1170. The Great Mosque of al-Nuri, built by [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] in 1172 with its leaning al-Hadba minaret, stood until its destruction in 2017.
zengid-dynasty-of-mosul.e: [[e:saladin|Saladin]] forced Izz al-Din Mas'ud to accept Ayyubid overlordship in 1186. The last Zengid rulers became figureheads for their minister Badr al-Din Lu'lu', who took power around 1233, founding the [[s:luluid-dynasty|Lu'lu'id dynasty]].

zhabdrung-bhutan.t: The state founded by the Tibetan lama Ngawang Namgyal that unified Bhutan under a dual system of religious and civil rule.
zhabdrung-bhutan.o: Ngawang Namgyal, a lama of the Drukpa school, fled [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] in 1616 after a dispute over his recognition as a reincarnation. In western [[s:kingdom-of-bhutan|Bhutan]] he built fortress-monasteries, or dzongs, including Simtokha and Punakha, repelled Tibetan invasions and unified the valleys, taking the title Zhabdrung.
zhabdrung-bhutan.r: The Zhabdrung created the dual system, chhoesi, in which a chief abbot, the Je Khenpo, led the monastic body while a civil ruler, the Druk Desi, governed, with regional governors called penlops. He codified laws and established Bhutanese identity. After his death, kept secret until about 1705, reincarnations of the Zhabdrung served as nominal heads.
zhabdrung-bhutan.e: Civil wars among penlops weakened central authority, and [[s:kingdom-of-bhutan|Bhutan]] lost the Duars lowlands to the British in the war of 1864 to 1865. Ugyen Wangchuck, penlop of Trongsa, emerged supreme, and in 1907 an assembly elected him hereditary king, creating the Kingdom of Bhutan.

zaporozhian-sich.t: The fortified island camp of the Zaporozhian Cossacks below the Dnieper rapids, a self-governing warrior republic and symbol of Ukrainian freedom.
zaporozhian-sich.o: From the 15th century runaway peasants, adventurers and townsmen gathered on the steppe frontier as [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]], fishing, hunting and fighting the [[e:tatars|Tatars]]. Around 1552 Prince Dmytro Vyshnevetsky built a fort on the island of Mala Khortytsia, often seen as the first Sich. Later Siches were built at several sites beyond the rapids, out of reach of royal officials.
zaporozhian-sich.r: The Sich was a male military community governed by a general assembly, the rada, which elected the kish otaman and other officers. [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] were [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] and lived in barracks by units called kurins. They raided Ottoman and Crimean coasts in light boats, served the [[s:polish-lithuanian-commonwealth|Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth]] for pay and often rebelled against it. [[e:bohdan-khmelnytsky|Bohdan Khmelnytsky's]] uprising began there in 1648.
zaporozhian-sich.e: [[e:peter-the-great|Peter I]] destroyed the Sich in 1709 because its [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] joined Mazepa. A new Sich was allowed in 1734, but in 1775 [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine II's]] army surrounded and abolished it, exiling the last otaman Petro Kalnyshevsky. Its Cossacks dispersed to the [[s:danube-sich|Danube Sich]] and later the [[s:black-sea-cossack-host|Black Sea Cossack Host]].

ziyadid-dynasty.t: The first Islamic dynasty of Yemen's coastal plain, which founded Zabid as its capital and ruled the Tihama for two centuries.
ziyadid-dynasty.o: In 818 or 819 the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] [[e:al-mamun|al-Ma'mun]] sent Muhammad ibn Ziyad, a descendant of the Umayyad governor Ziyad ibn Abihi, to subdue rebellious tribes in the Tihama. He founded the city of Zabid as his base and established a hereditary [[e:emirate|emirate]], recognising Abbasid [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]].
ziyadid-dynasty.r: The Ziyadids ruled the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] coastal plain and at times claimed authority over [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]] and the highlands. Zabid became a walled city and a leading centre of [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] learning. Real power often lay with African slave ministers; the Nubian Husayn ibn Salamah, regent in the late 10th century, built mosques and roads linking Zabid with [[e:mecca|Mecca]] and Hadramawt.
ziyadid-dynasty.e: In the early 11th century the last Ziyadid was a child under the control of slave commanders. The line ended around 1018, and after a struggle among these commanders Najah took Zabid around 1022, founding the [[s:najahid-dynasty|Najahid dynasty]]. Zabid's mosques and scholarly tradition survived and made it a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO]] World Heritage city.

zengid-dynasty.t: The Turkish dynasty of Zengi and Nur al-Din that united Muslim Syria against the Crusaders and prepared the way for Saladin.
zengid-dynasty.o: Imad al-Din Zengi, son of a Seljuk governor, was appointed atabeg of [[e:mosul|Mosul]] in 1127 and took [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] in 1128. In 1144 he captured [[s:county-of-edessa|Edessa]], destroying the County of Edessa's capital, before being murdered in 1146.
zengid-dynasty.r: His son [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] ruled from [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], took [[e:damascus|Damascus]] in 1154 and united [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. He promoted [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] revival with [[e:madrasa|madrasas]], the Nuri hospital in Damascus, and a court for complaints, and presented his wars as [[e:jihad|jihad]]. He sent [[e:shirkuh|Shirkuh]] and [[e:saladin|Saladin]] to [[e:egypt|Egypt]], where Saladin became [[e:vizier|vizier]] in 1169. Other Zengids ruled [[e:mosul|Mosul]], Sinjar and Jazirat ibn Umar as Turkish atabegs of a largely Arab and Kurdish population.
zengid-dynasty.e: After [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] died in 1174, [[e:saladin|Saladin]] took over [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and reduced the Zengid branches to [[e:vassal|vassals]]. The [[e:mosul|Mosul]] line lasted until Badr al-Din Lu'lu' displaced it in the 1230s, and minor branches survived until about 1250.

zhou-wu-sangui.t: The dynasty proclaimed by Wu Sangui, the general who let the Manchus into China and later rebelled against them, during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories.
zhou-wu-sangui.o: [[e:wu-sangui|Wu Sangui]], the Ming commander who opened the [[e:shanhai-pass|Shanhai Pass]] to the [[e:manchus|Manchus]] in 1644, conquered south-western [[e:china|China]] for the [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]], executed the last [[s:southern-ming|Southern Ming]] emperor in 1662 and ruled Yunnan and Guizhou almost independently as a feudatory prince. When the [[e:kangxi-emperor|Kangxi Emperor]] moved to abolish the feudatories in 1673, Wu rebelled, declaring a new [[s:wu-zhou|Zhou dynasty]].
zhou-wu-sangui.r: With Geng Jingzhong in Fujian and [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] Zhixin in Guangdong, Wu at first controlled most of southern [[e:china|China]], but his claim to restore Chinese rule was undermined by his own past. In 1678 he formally proclaimed himself emperor at Hengzhou (Hengyang) in Hunan. His regime was a military state financed by the resources of the south-west.
zhou-wu-sangui.e: [[e:wu-sangui|Wu Sangui]] died a few months after his enthronement in 1678. His grandson Wu Shifan retreated to Kunming as Qing armies advanced, and when the city fell in 1681 he killed himself, ending the revolt and opening the Qing consolidation of the south.

zhongshan.t: A kingdom founded by the Di people of Hebei that rose to call itself one of China's royal powers, known for the spectacular bronzes from King Cuo's tomb.
zhongshan.o: Zhongshan was founded by the Xianyu, a Baidi people who had settled in the Taihang foothills of central [[e:hebei|Hebei]]. Their state, known as Xianyu in Spring and Autumn sources, took the name Zhongshan in the 5th century BCE. Conquered by the [[s:state-of-wei|State of Wei]] around 407 BCE, it regained independence around 380 BCE and moved its capital to Lingshou.
zhongshan.r: Zhongshan adopted much of Chinese court culture while keeping its own customs. In 323 BCE its ruler joined four other states in proclaiming himself king. King Cuo's tomb at Pingshan, excavated in the 1970s, contained bronzes with long inscriptions, inlaid winged beasts and a bronze plan of the royal cemetery, the oldest known architectural drawing in [[e:china|China]].
zhongshan.e: After taking part in the invasion of the [[s:state-of-yan|State of Yan]] in 314 BCE, Zhongshan was gradually conquered by King Wuling of the [[s:state-of-zhao|State of Zhao]], who completed its annexation in 296 BCE. The Lingshou city walls and royal tombs survive near Pingshan, [[e:hebei|Hebei]].
